utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. We have been in recess for a few weeks while the other Trial Chamber was using this courtroom for another proceeding. We have, of course, missed counsel very much and the other parties. We are ready to resume today. I understand that we will first begin with the Defence motion regarding hearsay. The Defence has requested a hearing regarding this motion. We will then talk about general matters that the Judges want to bring to counsels' attention. Then I understand that the Prosecutor has an application that it wishes to present, perhaps in camera, and, depending upon the ruling on that application, we would hear the next witness in camera in closed session. No? I have been given wrong information on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It would not be the next witness, your Honour; it is a witness later on, but not the next witness.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Not the very next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The very next witness is ready to proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. Those are our plans for this morning, perhaps even into the afternoon. Mr. Wladimiroff, are you ready to proceed with your motion on hearsay?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, but Miss De Bertodano will present the argument.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, Miss Hollis will respond for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. MISS DE BERTODANO: Thank you, your Honours. Your Honours are aware that the question of hearsay evidence is a matter of continuing concern to the Defence. We have already made some objections about hearsay evidence. This motion, I would like to make clear, does not seek to go back over old ground but to anticipate matters yet to arise. Your Honours, because we consider it to be a major issue, we have requested there be oral argument on this matter. If I might start by outlining the motion? The relief we have requested is as follows, firstly, that the Tribunal refuse to hear evidence relating to the guilt of the accused which is not within the direct knowledge of the witness giving such evidence and, secondly, that the Tribunal have discretion to hear any evidence excluded by point 1 if it considers that its probative value substantially outweighs its prejudicial effect. Your Honours, I would stress at this point (and I fear there may have been a misunderstanding on this matter) that these two points go together. They are not alternatives. I only mention that because the Prosecution's response appears to assume that they are proposed as alternative measures and they are not. Your Honours, the effect of these measures would be that there was a change in the presumption with regard to hearsay, that is, that hearsay evidence would be excluded unless there was a reason to include it. Your Honours, this is a feature of all adversarial systems and it is one in recognition of the fact that hearsay is generally regarded to be evidence of secondary quality and that there is a preference for first hand evidence in criminal trials. The reasons for this preference are simple. Firstly, that first hand evidence is given in court under oath and, secondly, that the defendant can cross-examine witnesses on evidence that they have given of what they have directly seen or heard. The defendant loses his right to cross-examine witnesses when it comes to hearsay evidence, because the witness who made the statement is not present in court. Your Honours, I would quote at this point from paragraph 5 of the Defence motion Article 21.4(e) of the Statute of the Tribunal which affords the accused the right to examine or have examined the witnesses against him. Your Honours, in our submission, this suggests that evidence should be first hand. Your Honours, I would further mention that there are features peculiar to this particular trial which cause the Defence concern in relation to hearsay evidence. I would refer your Honours to paragraphs 10 and 11 of the Defence motion which briefly deal with the situation in the area at the time, the fear and confusion among witnesses, the length of time since hearsay statements have been made and the dramatic split between ethnic groups. Your Honour, the Prosecution has expressed concern that the Trial Chamber has not the power to grant the Defence motion without referring this to a full Chambers of Judges. Your Honours, in our submission, that is not the case. The Trial Chamber has very broad powers under Rules 89(C) and (D) to admit and exclude such evidence as it sees fit. If we can turn to 89(D) of the Rules, "A Chamber may exclude evidence if its probative value is substantially outweighed by the need to ensure a fair trial". Your Honours, we say that, as a general rule, the value of hearsay evidence is substantially outweighed by the need to ensure a fair trial. Your Honours, by making this ruling, you would not be binding future Trial Chambers, but your ruling would have value as a precedent for future Trial Chambers. So, your Honours, the substance of this motion is that, as a general rule, hearsay is unreliable. However, some types of hearsay have sufficient probative value to be admissible and those seeking to admit hearsay statements should show this to be the case. Your Honours, the Defence attached to its motion an article taken from a book called "War crimes in international law", and the article on hearsay evidence in war crimes trials is written by Kenneth Mann. Your Honour, I would draw your attention to two points in this article. Firstly, at the bottom of page 371 the last paragraph on that page demonstrates that under discretionary as opposed to bounded systems of evidence, and that would include systems in which there are no hearsay Rules, there are likely to be more false convictions due to the fact that the Prosecution is bound not to use evidence that it deems to be inculpatory. Your Honour, going on to pages 372 to 3 ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Would you just repeat that again? MISS DE BERTODANO: Sure. Your Honour, on page 371, I can read the paragraph, if that would assist? The paragraph starts: "To exemplify the way in which Rules of hearsay influence distribution of error, we can compare a hypothetical murder trial in which the Prosecution is limited to the extent to which it can present hearsay evidence with a murder trial in which the Prosecution is not limited to the same extent. It is quite clear that the limitation on Prosecution in the former system will result in the exclusion of evidence that the Prosecution views as inculpatory. In comparison, the Prosecutor in the discretionary system will not be so limited, that is, he will not have to exclude evidence he views as inculpatory to the same extent".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: But, with respect, that simply is stating the obvious; more comes in in one system than another. MISS DE BERTODANO: Your Honour, yes, I agree that it is stating the obvious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: It scarcely makes any point at all. MISS DE BERTODANO: Your Honour, I disagree, with respect. The point is that if hearsay evidence is not excluded, there will be evidence which comes in as part of the evidence in the trial which is prejudicial towards the Defence and which would be excluded in a trial in which hearsay evidence was not allowed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Surely. MISS DE BERTODANO: So it must be true that that ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: True but obvious. MISS DE BERTODANO: Your Honour, if you say so.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Your better quote from this article, it seems to me, is on the next page or the next two pages, 373, the last paragraph. MISS DE BERTODANO: I was going to turn to exactly that point, that bounded systems of evidence, i.e. ones in which there are more restricted Rules, can control the distribution of error better than unbounded systems and, therefore, any restrictions on hearsay are likely to prejudice the Prosecution to a greater extent than they prejudice the Defence. Your Honour, the article concludes that hearsay Rules are one of the specific Rules in which one can create fewer false convictions than false acquittals. So the system of error is regulated to that extent.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You are familiar though, of course, with a Rule, I think it is 404 of the Rules of Evidence in the United States, which would allow a court to exclude evidence if it had prejudicial effect. You know, it is kind of a balancing of relevant evidence, if it is outweighed by the prejudicial effect that it would have, could then be excluded. So I understand what this author says, but that is a Rule which he really does not address and the United States is a bounded system. Also, in our system we have a Rule 89(D) which would allow us to exclude evidence if its probative value is substantially outweighed by the need to ensure a fair trial -- "fair trial", not "prejudicial effect", "fair trial". MISS DE BERTODANO: Your Honour, this is why we seek to make this motion. Your Honour, we would seek to exclude hearsay evidence before it is heard by the Court, so that it is not a question of hearing it and then weighing up its prejudicial effect. It is a question of having argument beforehand as to whether such evidence ought to be heard before it is, in fact, decided that it can be heard by the Court. So if it was decided that there was no reason to include a piece of hearsay evidence, it would simply not be included.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You are not really arguing, are you, that all hearsay evidence should be excluded? Are you not arguing that hearsay evidence that does not fit within one of the exceptions --- MISS DE BERTODANO: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: -- recognised by common law systems -- I can only speak really for the United States, we have so many only exceptions that the Rules are almost swallowed up -- in any case, is it not your position that if the hearsay evidence does not fit one of these exceptions then it should not be admitted because it would have the prejudicial effect? MISS DE BERTODANO: Your Honour, yes, but one does not have to hear the hearsay evidence, hear the content of the hearsay evidence before deciding whether it fits one of the exceptions or not.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: How would we accomplish that? If we did not know whether the person was going to testify, for example, because of an excited utterance -- because that was one of the issues, one of the two hearsay objections that we have overruled of the Defence thus far -- until we hear the witness testify, unless perhaps the Prosecution can be required to make an offer of proof as to what a witness will testify to, we do not know whether it would fit within the exception. MISS DE BERTODANO: Your Honour, with respect, I do not agree. The Prosecution, by and large, knows what its witnesses are going to be able to testify to; to a great extent we also know what the Prosecution witnesses will be able to testify to because we have their statements. My suggestion would be that when a point on hearsay seemed to be about to arise, which would be obvious to the Prosecutor who was examining the witness, then would be the time to say, "Your Honours, there is a point on hearsay. This witness is going to testify that A told him something concerning the defendant in these conditions". You would not actually have to hear the content of the piece of hearsay to decide whether it was, for example, an excited utterance. Your Honour, of course, there would be slips -- there are always slips in the best regulated systems -- but, by and large, it seems to me that would be the best way in which to hear objections to hearsay.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Even in bounded systems, though, the lawyers do not run the show. The Judges have to make the decisions as to the admissibility of evidence. It just seems to me that it would be very difficult for us to make that decision. The Prosecutor knows best what, I suppose, the witness will testify to. The Defence has a good idea of what the witness will testify to because of the statements that you have. But I understand your position. MISS DE BERTODANO: Yes. Your Honour, I would just add that if the Bench is going to hear the evidence anyway, then there is very little point to this motion. This motion is specifically to exclude the hearing of such evidence, not simply to limit the weight attached to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I am right, am I not, in thinking that the reason for that approach by bounded systems is that the minds of the jury will be adversely affected by receiving the evidence in the first instance, and that that prejudice will not be able to be dispelled by any subsequent decision that it should really be excluded, therefore, you have a voir dire procedure? MISS DE BERTODANO: Your Honour, yes, and the jury is out while this is heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: All that is totally foreign to the way in which we operate. MISS DE BERTODANO: Your Honour, yes. This is different in a sense it is a Bench trial, not a jury trial. So we have a kind of mixed system in which we have an adversarial system which is generally associated with jury trials, yet we also have a Bench trial.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: In your papers you have said that even in Bench trials, however, in the bounded systems, this hearsay evidence that did not, I gather, fit one of the exceptions to hearsay would be excluded as well. MISS DE BERTODANO: Your Honour, yes, in my system, if you have Magistrates' trials or on appeal, if you hear more evidence, the Judge can still not hear hearsay evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Except that, as a matter of practice, and each of we, Judges, have all been Judges before we came to the Tribunal, at least based on my experience, as a matter of practice, the Rules regarded the admission of hearsay and other matters as well are much more relaxed because there is this theory that Judges have this ability that jurors do not have to sometimes disregard what the Cardinal might say, referring to an earlier motion that was argued, I believe, by Mr. Kay. So at least there is this belief -- whether it is well-founded or not -- that the Rules regarding the admission of evidence operate differently if there is a Bench trial -- at least in my system. MISS DE BERTODANO: Your Honour, yes, I would entirely agree with that and for this reason, our motion is proposing a very broad discretion in that the Judges can elect to hear any hearsay evidence provided they deem that its probative value, there is some kind of guarantee, some extra guarantee of its trustworthiness which is the general sense behind most hearsay exceptions, that there is something extra which suggests that it will be trustworthy; whether because it is an excited utterance or because it is a dying declaration or whatever it is. It was those points on which I was suggesting that the Judges could decide without actually hearing the content of the statement. But, your Honour, we accept fully that this is not a jury trial; partly because of this, we have limited the hearsay motion to evidence which directly concerns the guilt of the accused. Again I feel from the Prosecution response there may have been some misunderstanding about that. Your Honour, the intention was that we would use this motion only with regard to evidence which directly implicated the accused in one of the crimes with which he is charged. The broader issues of the conflict and so forth, we have not sought to introduce any kind of hearsay rule at all.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What do you mean by that, because if you are talking about evidence that would specifically connect the accused with a charged offence --- MISS DE BERTODANO: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: -- that is what you are talking about? MISS DE BERTODANO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Because this is a war crimes tribunal, since we will be hearing cases involving serious violations of international humanitarian law, there is more that has to be offered than in a typical murder trial or theft trial or whatever, you know, there is more that must be offered than just, "I saw the defendant". You have to put it in the context of an international or armed conflict -- international if we are talking about Article 2, grave breaches; armed conflict if we are talking about the other Articles. So, in order for the Prosecutor to establish guilt, it must do more than just place the accused at the scene or offer evidence that someone saw the accused commit an offence. They have to go further and that is the kind of evidence that we have been hearing. We have finished with policy witnesses -- thank goodness --- MISS DE BERTODANO: Your Honour, that is why we bring up -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: -- but we are still on count 1 and that is persecution, and there are a number of matters that the Prosecutor has been attempting to offer, multiplicity of acts, whether it was directed at a particular religious or political group. So that goes to the guilt of the accused; it does not certainly make him guilty if there is not that other piece. MISS DE BERTODANO: Your Honour, in that case that is my fault for the phrasing of the motion. My intention was specifically to restrict it to matters as to whether the accused himself was participating in the crimes. Therefore, we have not made any objections to hearsay during the weeks when we were hearing about the background and the historical nature of the conflict. Our concern is not with regard to the prejudice that may or may not be there when people are talking about the more general issues, but with regard to the prejudice that may be there when people are talking about the accused's participation. Because, your Honour, when it comes to hearsay evidence, we are not able to cross-examine the witness who says the defendant was there if that evidence comes to us through another person. We do not know what the motives of the witness would be for saying that the defendant was there, but in this type of situation, which may be unique in criminal trials where there is this deep ethnic hatred, we would not like the accused to be prejudiced by the prejudices of others who are not available to give evidence, unless there is a very good reason.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Would you give us a list of exceptions that you would consider would be appropriate? MISS DE BERTODANO: Your Honour, no, we specifically did not want to limit your Honours in deciding what exceptions you thought were appropriate by reference to, say, a particular set of national Rules. There may be any number of reasons why you think it would be appropriate to hear a certain piece of hearsay evidence and we do not seek to anticipate those situations.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: How then would it operate? Once again, the Prosecutor would offer a witness and, based on the statements you have received regarding that witness, you would say, "This evidence that the Prosecutor is seeking to offer is hearsay" and, if I understand your papers correctly, it does not fit within the generally recognised exceptions to hearsay that would allow this testimony to be admissible because it is trustworthy and reliable, and then we might say to you, "Well, what exception are you talking about when you say it does not fit within any of the exceptions?" Do you understand my question? MISS DE BERTODANO: I think I understand the question and I think I can answer it like this, that we would not be making objections based on reference to a specified set of exceptions. It might well be that exceptions which are commonly used in many systems such as excited utterance might come up. In that case, that could be used as a way of your Honours hearing that evidence. But if there were another reason which does not appear in any of these systems why you felt that it was more trustworthy than the common run of hearsay evidence, we would not seek for a moment to tie your hands in allowing it in.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. The United States has 24 exceptions and I am not sure what is the situation in Australia and Malaysia, but remember we are one Trial Chamber but we operate under Rules that have been adopted by the Tribunal that govern the other Trial Chamber as well as the Appeals Chamber. So now would you suggest that the three of us get together, examine our systems, see whether any of those systems are recognised? MISS DE BERTODANO: Your Honour, I do not see any need to do it in anticipation of these matters coming up. Your Honour, as I see, it will happen as and when these issues arise and there is an attempt to present hearsay evidence. That would seem to me to be the easiest way of dealing with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Can I just take you up on that? How would you suggest, if we accede to your submission, that we interpret Rule 89(D)? We would exclude evidence if, and how would it go on then? MISS DE BERTODANO: Your Honour, we are not seeking to change the Rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Exactly. It seems to me that already you have the situation that you are arguing for if you read and understand 89(D), which says that if its probative value is substantially outweighed by the need to ensure a fair trial. I think you started off by saying really it is the onus of proof that is changed. That is what I would like you to explain to me. MISS DE BERTODANO: Your Honour, yes. What I said was that we could read it that the probative value of hearsay evidence in general is substantially outweighed by the need to ensure a fair trial. However, there may be circumstances in which it is desirable for hearsay evidence to be included and those would constitute the exceptions. But, your Honour, I do not see that that requires making any change to the Rules. The change in terms of procedure would be that there would be a direction that when a point of hearsay was to arise this would automatically be raised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes, so that the fact that you stand up at some stage and say, "A point of hearsay is now about to be given, we know that from the fact that we have the statement of the witness", and you would at that stage seek, without the evidence having been heard, a determination by the Bench as to whether there is an outweighing of probative value by the need to have a fair trial? MISS DE BERTODANO: Your Honour, yes, because, in general, the reason that hearsay falls into one of the exceptions has nothing to do with the content of the statement, so what this would really change is that we would not need to wait until the statement had been made before we made this kind of objection. We would automatically have a rule by which hearsay was excluded, unless there was a reason to include it, rather than the other way around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: The difficulty, surely, is going to be that which the Presiding Judge has mentioned, how do we come to a conclusion on that balancing exercise without hearing the evidence? You will know what it is, the Prosecution, of course, will know what it is; we will not because we will not have heard it and there will not be a voir dire process. MISS DE BERTODANO: Surely, your Honour, it would be quite possible for you to be given the circumstances ---

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: A description. MISS DE BERTODANO: -- in which this hearsay evidence was heard without being given the content of the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: It does not seem to me that your motion really would change anything, because that is the situation that would arise if you make an objection in relation to some particularly obvious case of prejudice and absence of substantial probative value. MISS DE BERTODANO: Your Honour, I think that the change would be that the objection to hearsay would be automatic, and that it would automatically happen that the hearsay was not heard until it had been decided there was a good reason for it to be heard. But, your Honour, you are right in the sense that it makes no difference to your discretion. You can decide to hear or not to hear anything that you choose and we have made no attempt to limit that discretion ---

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I appreciate that. MISS DE BERTODANO: -- and that was with reason.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Let me just share something with you, if I may, that relates to the adoption of the Rules: The Judges drafted the Rules and we drafted them together as being Judges from common law systems, civil law systems, in an attempt, as we have said, to get the best of all systems, but a system that would be most appropriate for this peculiar (in the good sense) Tribunal. This is the first and we wanted to have Rules that would address this kind of Tribunal. During those discussions, one Judge stated that, in principle, regarding this rule anything would be admissible. I want to tell you what I said because I do not think that we are so far away from your position. I said that all out of court statements should not automatically be admissible, should not automatically be admissible; instead I enquired as to the meaning of the word "probative", and was that included, was that meant to include such matters as truthfulness, voluntariness and the trustworthiness of the evidence? All of the Judges concluded that to be so. So that when we put the word "probative" in there, all of the Judges agreed that implicit in the word "probative", which allows us to admit any relevant evidence that has probative value, would be trustfulness, voluntariness and trustworthiness; and that in making the decision as to whether the evidence is probative, it will involve a consideration such as truthfulness, voluntariness and trustworthiness. That gets you, it seems to me, where you want to be, except that it would not allow for an automatic exclusion of all hearsay evidence unless it fits within an exception recognised by this Chamber or by common law systems generally. It does not get you that far, but it gives you some latitude in that if we consider that the evidence is lacking in trustworthiness, that it is not truthful, then it has no probative value. But back to what Judge Stephen says, I do not know how we would decide that until we hear it. MISS DE BERTODANO: Your Honour, yes. For us, that is a crucial point and that is why we seek for the automatic restriction on hearsay and the need for those who wish to adduce hearsay to show that there is a good reason for it being adduced, because we think it is fundamental that the Trial Chamber should not hear evidence which is unreliable. Your Honour, this comes back to a point which has often been raised of justice being seen to be done as well as simply being done. Your Honour, I would suggest that we are well aware that this is a Bench trial, but there are problems attendant on Bench trials which are not problems experienced by jury trials, and one of those is that the tribunal of law and the tribunal of fact are the same people. Because of that, the person who decides whether or not evidence will be admitted is the same person as the person who then evaluates the evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Except that in continental systems, and there is an entirely different system other than common law system; we come from common law systems but there is another whole world out there, continental systems, and we have Judges from civil law systems, France is one of them and Judge Jorda is the Presiding Judge of the other Trial Chamber. I would never suggest to Judge Jorda that justice is not done or even appear to be done in his system when, if you were in their system, we would not be having this discussion about the admissibility of hearsay, because it is done routinely. They do not even fathom our approach to this. They sincerely believe that that is a better system, that that is a search for the truth, the actual truth, as opposed to trial truth, as they say about common law systems -- maybe I should not describe too much because I am not a civil lawyer. MISS DE BERTODANO: But then, your Honour, those continental systems are largely investigative systems rather than the sort of adversarial system that we have here. In a system where we have live witnesses who are cross-examined in the court, it seems to me to be more necessary to have Rules which do exclude certain types of unreliable evidence than in systems where the evidence is largely documentary.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It is largely documentary based upon what the investigating Magistrate Judge has done, secured the statements and prepared the dossier, gives it to both counsel, but we three have visited a civil law system and we saw a lot of cross-examination from the Judge though. MISS DE BERTODANO: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So there there is a whole different system, but OK. You want us to adopt the common law system in this Chamber and I gather throughout the Tribunal because of the need for justice and the appearance of justice. MISS DE BERTODANO: Your Honour, we are talking with regard to this specific trial, whether it is adopted by other Trial Chambers is not our affair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Could I ask you this? Are you really asking for more than this, that when a stage comes in the course of evidence being given by the Prosecution which you think raises hearsay and you then stand up and say, "Now, there is going to be some hearsay evidence being given, and it is of a character which would be substantially outweighed by the need to ensure a fair trial, therefore, you should not hear it", and you then describe that evidence and you then seek a ruling? That is really all that you are seeking, is it not? MISS DE BERTODANO: Your Honour, yes, except that we have put it the other way round in that it is not for us to say, to give reasons, why it is of a character that substantially outweighs a fair trial. It is for those seeking to adduce it to give reasons why it should be included and that is the crucial difference. Your Honour, I can make some points on the Prosecution material, if that would assist, before the Prosecution presents its motion, or I can leave that until after.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Let me clarify your position. In your paper you used the term "fair trial", I mean prejudicial effect -- let me see if I can find it. It is the second relief requested, that the Tribunal have the discretion to hear any evidence excluded by (1) if it considers that its probative value substantially outweighs its prejudicial effect. You have kind of rewritten our Rule 89(C). 89(C) says, "A Chamber may exclude evidence if its probative value is substantially outweighed by the need to ensure a fair trial". Is that a significant difference or am I misreading it? MISS DE BERTODANO: Your Honour, it turns it round; it turns it round because it makes the assumption that there is prejudicial effect inherent in hearsay. If it were felt better to substitute the word "substantially" -- it cannot be done with any great ease, the substitution of words, therefore, "prejudicial effect" seemed to me to illustrate the problem with hearsay, which is that it does have prejudicial effect, it is secondary quality evidence. The main effect of Rule 2 is that it turns around the hearsay Rules as they stand.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: 89(C)? MISS DE BERTODANO: It does not turn around any of the Rules as such, but it turns around the way in which one considers hearsay evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Miss de Bertodano, do you have any additional submissions? MISS DE BERTODANO: Your Honour, no. My only additional points were on the Prosecution response and you may feel that you would wish to hear the Prosecution first.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will do that. We will hear from the Prosecution and then you may respond or add to it. Yes, from the Prosecutor, please?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Your Honours, we noted in our response to this motion we believe that, in essence, what we are talking about here is adoption of a new Rule and a substantial amendment to an existing Rule. We would suggest that the Rules that are in place now are more than appropriate to provide this accused with a fair trial and, in fact, are tailored specifically to this Tribunal where we have experienced Judges hearing the evidence. Rules of evidence to a great extent are always a matter of policy and balancing test. Unless you are at either end of the spectrum, one end being excluding all evidence, on the other end being denying an accused a fair trial, where that balance is struck in the middle relies in great part upon the setting in which the trial will be heard and upon answers to policy questions. Certainly each national jurisdiction determines how it will balance those competing interests. At this Tribunal -- you, Judges, know much better than the Prosecution or the Defence -- clearly these Judges, all of the Judges, have decided where that balance will be struck. The balance has been struck in favour of admissibility of evidence relying upon what is always presumed of Judges, that is, that Judges know the law, they apply the law, they are able when appropriate to hear evidence and then exclude it or to determine what weight is to be given to that evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: With all due respect to that suggestion and respect to any of my fellow Judges, I do not know, maybe the Judges are given a little too much -- what is the word -- wisdom. That is certainly what we hear but, you know, Judges are people and we are people too. We all have our own life experiences and our ways of approaching things. But I hear that all the time and I suppose that is what is accepted so we will do that.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that certainly was accepted, although probably every one of us in this room has had occasion to doubt that at some time. It is said with no disrespect at all. However, the point is, yes, you are people, but any criminal justice system is made up of people. The point has been made that Judges are uniquely qualified to be able to set aside passions, prejudices and act as objectively as humanly possible on evidence. I believe that is why we have that balance. So here the balance has been struck, clearly, in favour of admissibility. What the Defence is proposing to you in many ways would restrict what you get even more than national systems (which have very bounded Rules) would allow you to get. For example, in bounded systems there is a rule excluding hearsay, but there are many, many exceptions. If hearsay falls within an exception, there is no requirement then to go on to the balancing test that the Defence says you must do in order to get in hearsay. So that is more restrictive. The Defence says you cannot even hear the evidence you are to exclude. I am not aware of any bounded system where the Judges are precluded from hearing that evidence that is in dispute, even if it is a Judge alone trial where they then must not consider it if they exclude it. So they are going very far away from what you, Judges, have decided is appropriate for you at this Tribunal and are in many ways even more restrictive as to what evidence you receive than would be the case in a bounded system. As far as the uniqueness of this trial, we would suggest that the concerns set forth in paragraphs 10 and 11 are concerns Trial Chambers are going to face here and in every trial that they hear, so there is nothing unique about that. It is somewhat confusing about this test that is to be applied here, if you adopt this rule, a per se hearsay exclusion rule, with no exceptions (which most systems do not adopt, they have specified exceptions), if you do adopt this exclusion rule, then the Defence says, "Well, the Prosecution and the Defence can get together and decide what hearsay will non-the-less come before you which will be, of course, a violation of the per se exclusion rule. But since they would not object, somehow that would come in. So it is a little confusing how that would work. It appears what would happen if this per se exclusion rule is adopted is that this Trial Chamber and the other Trial Chamber would then have to set upon re-establishing what exceptions there are to the hearsay rules. We suggest that in this setting that really would be an inefficient use of time and resources at this Tribunal. In that regard, in so far as the Defence has argued that even as Judges, of course, you should not hear this evidence, that in bounded systems you would hear, but you should not hear it because it is so prejudicial and could lead to more convictions than acquittals, it is interesting to note that the case upon which the article relied that they submitted to you, the Demjanjuk case, that was eventually set aside because of hearsay evidence that was admitted at the appellate stage. So, in fact, it was hearsay evidence that had that earlier conviction set aside.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If I understand that article correctly, the author, at least, proposes that there be a bounded system but that it be applied differently for the Defence than the Prosecution, but you are correct, on the appellate level they applied the discretionary system for sure because it did not fit within any exception.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: That is right. They, in fact, in that case upheld the inclusion, the admission, of the hearsay at the trial level, but they said, "Because of this additional hearsay we have been given, we now find a reasonable doubt and we have to set it aside". So they did not say in that case that hearsay is invalid; in fact, they used hearsay to set aside that earlier conviction and appropriately so, but the point being even in the bounded systems -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The reason, though, is that they would apply a different system for the accused -- maybe I misspoke when I said bounded for the Prosecution -- bounded for the accused but applied differently; was it the conclusion of that author, at least, that the decision was right because there should be a different system for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I think that author uses this case to show the dangers of hearsay evidence. As far as whether there should be a different system for the Defence and the Prosecution, I would suggest that when we are talking about Rules of evidence that are used to determine the trustworthiness and the probative value of evidence, that it should be the same Rules because the ultimate question is, the evidence before you, whether it is Prosecution evidence or Defence evidence, is it sufficiently trustworthy that it should be considered at all for whatever point it is being offered? So I would suggest that would not differ, depending on whether it was Prosecution or Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You see, the author says, "If war crimes trials are to create a strong and systematic barrier against false convictions, then the war crimes tribunal should choose bounded rules for both prosecution and defence, but these rules should be asymmetrical rules in which the defence would be allowed to present to the Court hearsay evidence which the prosecution would not be allowed to present. A proposed rule on these points would state that hearsay evidence is admissible by the prosecution in war crimes trials only when it fits exceptions applicable to the exclusionary rules in regular criminal trials of a national jurisdiction sponsoring the Court", which was Israel and, of course, we know in Israel, in ordinary crimes, they did not apply these -- but they would apply exclusionary rules but they did not in the war crimes tribunal, which is not our situation. He goes on: "In distinction, hearsay that may raise a reasonable doubt in the findings of the fact-finder on the issue of guilt may be presented by the defence even when it does not meet conventional exceptions to the hearsay rule". I do not know -- I have difficulty understanding that.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I have difficulty with that as well. I would suggest that the ultimate test, certainly in the United States with the catch all exception, they say, "Even if it is not a well-established exception to the hearsay rule, we know that the law evolves, so if you can prove sufficient inditia of reliability, we will allow it in". I would suggest that that should apply, if there is such a rule, to both the Prosecution and the Defence because the accused does not have a right to provide untrustworthy, unprobative evidence to any court. That is not a fundamental right of an accused. So when we are talking about what is admissible, what the bottom line is, the rule should apply equally. What the Defence is doing with their rules, I would suggest, is ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The Defence says it should not apply equally because you have the burden.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Of course we have the burden.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: And we should hold you to that burden.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: And you should. But when it comes to what evidence is admitted, the bottom line for all that, we would suggest, is that the Court should get evidence that is probative and, as you pointed out, probative evidence, there is a wide range of it, but the fundamental bottom line for probative evidence is that it is sufficiently trustworthy, sufficiently voluntary, sufficiently reliable. No matter which side presents evidence that is not sufficiently trustworthy, not sufficiently voluntary, not sufficiently reliable, that evidence should be excluded because it is of no assistance to anyone. So, when it comes to determining what the bottom line is for admissibility, that should not change whether it is the accused or the Prosecution. The accused has no right to present to you false testimony. He has no right to present to you untrustworthy testimony simply because it is the Defence. That is a very different issue than us having the burden of proof. The Defence test here, they say that their second part is not an alternative, but the first part seeks to exclude all hearsay evidence, period. They do not say anywhere in that first rule "except where both sides would agree that it meets within an exception". So it appears that if you take that first rule, then you never get to a balancing test, because if it is in any way hearsay it goes out. Even assuming that somehow they would put in a caveat that if it falls within a well-accepted or well-known exception, then it would come in, the second part that they offer to you, their second request substantially changes Rule 89(D) in the two ways that have previously been discussed. Rule 89(D), very appropriately, is a rule of admissibility because the people getting evidence are you, Judges. So it favours admissibility. The onus is on the opponent of the evidence to show why the evidence should not come in. The Defence test would put the onus upon the proponent of the evidence to justify its admissibility. That is a significant change. The test itself is significantly changed. We should hope that all of the evidence we provide, if it is relevant and probative, will have prejudicial effect, that is, will lead to proof beyond a reasonable doubt that this accused is guilty. That is not the test in 89(D). The test in 89(D) is that the Defence must show to exclude evidence that the need to ensure a fair trial -- a much higher standard -- requires its exclusion because that need substantially outweighs the value of the evidence to be admitted. So they are not only changing the burden, they are changing the test in a very substantial way. Basically, your Honours, what we suggest is the Rules as they exist allow this Tribunal to receive a great deal of evidence and rely upon the Judges' training, experience, professionalism, to determine what weight to give that evidence. If the Defence should make a showing that evidence that is being offered, that the need to ensure a fair trial substantially outweighs the value of that evidence, then 89(D) allows this court to exclude that evidence and then assumes that the court will not consider that evidence once it is excluded. That is consistent with bounded systems. In a sense, this is a somewhat bounded system because there are boundaries and 89(D) is the boundary, but because of the setting in which these trials are heard, it is a boundary which favours admissibility. The concerns that the Defence raises, even in 10 and 11 and the other concerns, are concerns they can raise in cross-examination. They can ask questions that will show this Chamber -- if the Chamber agrees with their questioning and responses will show this Chamber they should give little weight to the evidence that is being adduced, or they can make the argument under 89(D) and ask that this Chamber exclude the evidence. But the rule favouring admissibility is appropriate for this setting. It is appropriate for these trials. We would ask that you deny the Defence motion.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any response, Miss de Bertodano? MISS DE BERTODANO: Your Honour, only briefly. I do not understand the reading of the motion which says that point 1 is a complete exclusion. I thought the caveat in 2 was self-explanatory. I thought that I had dealt with that in my argument. Your Honours, this trial may not be unique among war crimes trials. It is, however, an extremely unusual situation among the normal run of criminal trials. The problems which this has given rise to which we have outlined in our argument, because we are dealing with hearsay, cannot be dealt with by cross-examination. That is precisely the point. When it comes to hearsay evidence, we do not have the power to cross-examine the person who made the original statement. Your Honour, for the reasons I have given, I would say that we are not changing the tests substantially. Again I think that I have dealt with that in sufficient detail not to need to go over it again. Your Honour, I would close by saying that we seek to have a trial which uses the best possible evidence so that there is no possibility of any insinuation that this has been a trial by rumour rather than by evidence. Most systems accept that evidence may be both relevant and probative but still inadmissible for obvious reasons. It is for that reason that we ask you to accept our motion.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The article you have given us relates to a war crimes tribunal where the evidence that was received dated back 40 years or so, I guess --- MISS DE BERTODANO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: -- it is that approximate date. Of course, the author there is concerned about the lapses of memory and other considerations. You state that that is a concern of yours in this motion, except that we are going back for a shorter period of time, obviously --- MISS DE BERTODANO: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: -- but still three years, four years perhaps, maybe even five, but that is one of your concerns. I do not know whether that is a neat fit with the situation proposed by the author regarding the war crimes trial in Israel. MISS DE BERTODANO: Your Honour, no. I was not seeking to show that there is any kind of direct fit with the Demjanjuk trial. It is a quite different situation. Your Honour, lapses in memory are relative. One can forget a great deal over four years; one can forget a great deal more over 40 years. It is a still a matter of concern for us, particularly in the light of the traumatic situations which have been suffered by a lot of witnesses which are known to have effects on powers of memory.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I understand that and I like the way you put that in your motion, but most criminal trials where there are victims, personal victims, individuals who have been victimized and, perhaps, even institutions that have been victimized, I think Judges are wise enough and experienced enough to know that there may be a reason sometimes for witnesses who appear before that court to have lapses, should I say. What we are hearing is extraordinary, not unprecedented, unfortunately, but that happens in national systems as well. So, I mean, the same considerations apply and in civil systems the same considerations apply and they are not constrained by the hearsay Rules. MISS DE BERTODANO: Your Honour, yes, but I would stress the uniqueness of the situation in which there has been such a bitter civil war.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Sure. It is unique, because everything is unique, but this is particularly unique, I suppose. You say you cannot cross-examine a proponent and, therefore, you want to exclude hearsay. You cannot cross-examine a proponent when hearsay is admitted by virtue of an exception in certain systems either. MISS DE BERTODANO: Your Honour, no, but the reason for most exceptions to hearsay is that there is some extra boost to reliability.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So then would you accept the proposition that this Tribunal has accepted and that is when we use the word "probative" we are talking about testimony which is truthful, voluntary and trustworthy? MISS DE BERTODANO: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That can be done even if it is hearsay. That is my suggestion. MISS DE BERTODANO: Your Honour, yes. This is why we say we are not making an actual change to the rules. We are seeking to change the way in which hearsay is dealt with.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is a decision will be made before we hear the testimony and we would then decide whether it fits within one of the exceptions generally accepted --- MISS DE BERTODANO: That you choose to recognise.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: -- that we choose to recognise? MISS DE BERTODANO: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Regarding 89(D), the decision that the majority of the Chamber issued in August of last year on protective measures, August 10th or 15th, whatever it was, but it was on protective measures requested by the Prosecutor regarding anonymity to be given to some of the witnesses, that decision, as I recall, gave anonymity to one of three witnesses to a particular incident, and then gave kind of a modified anonymity to two witnesses, but still gave their locality after the Defence had said, "We really do not need their names but we do need to know where they live". The majority said, "We will not give you the exact address, but we will give you a locality". As to the other witness that was anonymous, it was one of three witnesses, but we were careful in that decision to say that 89(D) would give us the ability to hear this evidence, place it in context and then make a determination as to whether or not the probative value of that evidence is substantially outweighed by the need to have a fair trial. So what we are saying is, "It will come in, but when we look at it all, we will make that determination". Now, you disagree, obviously, with the result reached in the decision, or maybe all of it or certainly a part of it, but that is the approach that we seek to apply in this instance and in all evidentiary matters, that is, we will take a look at it, see how it comes in, what is the context and then make this assessment, because there may be a prejudice occurring during trials, errors that are made by Judges, that do not reach the level of making the trial unfair. There is a concept of reversible error and non-reversible error in some systems, so that Judges may make errors but they are not reversible because it does not affect the fairness of the trial. That is what bothers me when you use the term "prejudicial" as opposed to "fair trial". We, at least, have taken the position, our Rules and at least the majority in a decision on anonymity, we will look at it in its entirety and make that decision. That is not satisfactory to you, I suppose? MISS DE BERTODANO: Your Honour, we are concerned that this is not only a fair trial but is seen to be a fair trial. This is a trial taking place in public and we are concerned that it is not seen to be a trial where unreliable evidence is heard.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: In civil systems then, I gather, those are not fair trials -- Mr. Wladimiroff, you come from a civil system. I do not want you to testify necessarily, but I am sure that you are very proud of your system; it has its defects like we all have in our systems. But do you want to respond to my suggestions about civil law systems because you certainly know about it and I do not?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, your Honour, the judges will cut off a witness who is going to reveal to the judge information that is passed to a witness by others. The judges would rather prefer to hear the other witness.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So you are saying that hearsay evidence is automatically excluded in the Dutch system?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Unless the judge is satisfied that the information which is passed to the Judge is reliable, and the same test will be applied there.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: How does that judge make that determination then in the actual trial setting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Invited by each of the parties.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Arguments from counsel? A judge does not listen to the testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: The testimony may come in, but the judges themselves will trigger the matter until the parties had triggered the matter at the earlier stage.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So if the parties trigger the matter at an earlier stage, does the judge then typically say, "Well, I hear from counsel but let me hear what this witness has to say so that I can rule"?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That is more or less case law, I would say, but it may depend on what the witness has said so far, whether the judge will stop him giving evidence and rather prefer the original information.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly to say that that the judges sometimes would hear the testimony of a witness that is objected to by defence on the grounds of hearsay in order to make a ruling as to whether that evidence should be heard?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Sometimes they will let the evidence come in to the extent that they are able to decide the issue. That is not a general rule as such, but it may depend on what has been said so far.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But in so far what was being said is that it is clear that this should not be admissible?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: At the end of it the judge may say, "We will not accept it; it is not admissible".

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I suppose my point was only to Miss de Bertodano, and I do not want to beat the point, is that this Tribunal, the first International Criminal Tribunal, is international and it is not a Malaysian tribunal, it is not an American tribunal, it is not an Australian tribunal, it is not a common law tribunal, common law system tribunal, it is not a civil law system tribunal; it is an amalgamation of both and intentionally done so because we expect the trials to come from all over the world, the Judges are from all over the world, and we are attempting to combine the systems. I believe that fair trials are given in civil law systems and they do have not this discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: We appreciate that, your Honours. The only thing we are looking for is a policy to develop what are the exceptions here where the Rules only provide that after coming in of the evidence you will apply 89(C) and (D). So what we are looking for is one step back, if there is any way to label, to identify, what are the exceptions for hearsay Rules here. We propose the policy not to accept hearsay evidence unless you have recognised an exception, because we have no exceptions here, we have no domestic rules. We are not bound in that respect. The next step is 89, we want one step back; before you are going to weigh the evidence, we want you to develop a policy on exceptions and we do not know where we stand. We only know that you will accept it unless we object.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Let me say this. It is difficult and we, Judges, will have to confer and decide how we will rule on this motion, but when you state that you want us to make a determination that the evidence would not come in unless it meets one of the exceptions, we are really back where we started from, because if there is no rule on hearsay, there are no exceptions, so we are kind of arguing in a circle. But I think you have your answer in that 89(C) says, "A Chamber may admit any relevant evidence which it deems to have probative value". That is not 89(D). 89(D) is the one that Miss De Bertodano suggests that we have kind of turned on its head, saying, "Oh, well, you know, we will make this determination later". I understand her position on that. But 89(C) is what guides us in the first instance when the evidence is coming in. What guides us is whether the evidence is relevant and whether it deems to have probative value. I suggest to counsel that probative value means being truthful, being voluntary and being trustworthy. Now, at least in my system, the underlying principle behind all of the exceptions is that, and others perhaps, but that is basically it, and reliability. So we accept, I think -- I certainly accept -- that that should be the standard. So we do not read to write "excited utterance" as an exception or res gestae you said in the Malaysian system or in the English system even or business records or all of those other -- or even the catch all. Do not think we are acting in a vacuum and that we are just making up rules we go along. We, as a tribunal, plenary met -- I think we have considered the Rules on eight different occasions, but we, believe me, have laboured hard and long with influences coming from different systems and different professions among the Judges and have come up with what we consider to be fair. I submit that if we admit evidence that is truthful, voluntary, trustworthiness with an underlining guide being reliability, that is probative and that fits 89(C). We do not get to 89(D) unless we, perhaps, make an error that the Defence would suggest or an error that the Prosecutor would suggest and then we say, "OK, we said it was probative but now we find that it is substantially outweighed by the need to have a fair trial, so although we said it was probative, we are going to exclude it". That is when we get to that kind of back door approach that is objected to by counsel, and I understand her position, but we do not get there if we apply 89(C) right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: We fully appreciate that, your Honour. May I just say to bring things back to the basic idea, the basic idea is that this is the first case. There is no case law except for two rulings in this case on hearsay evidence. It is essential in this case that we have a clear view of what is your position on hearsay evidence since we know by the disclosure of the statements given by the Prosecution to the Defence that we are going to deal with a lot of hearsay evidence in this case. It is our concern to know exactly where we stand. The basic, what we are looking for, is who is going to trigger what; are we going to learn afterwards what is your position according 89(C) or are we aware before that what your position might be? What we simply suggest is to have the issue triggered immediately so we know exactly where we stand, and not by us raising each time over and over again an objection. We want to label the problem the moment it is raised. That is exactly what we want. It is not allowed unless you rule it is; it is a policy to learn what are the exceptions here in your policy of executing 89(C) because we do not know, we do not know anything. We are just in a blank here. That is exactly what we want.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is what I attempted to do by reading -- I do not know whether it was appropriate, but our minutes are open where we discussed Rules and they are public. We, Judges, will confer and issue an order or a decision that I think will give you guidance. You are entitled to that. Probative, what does "probative" mean? I guess that is where you are. What does that mean? You want to know what it means so that you can phrase your arguments, your objections in a way that, hopefully, will be accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Because if we are going to object, based on what? We have no guidance here.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Judge Vohrah does not really have any additional questions. We have talked some matters and I think we have spent enough time on this. We would normally recess at 11.30. I am sure everyone is tired at this point. Maybe an early recess might be appropriate. We will rule very shortly on your motion, Mr. Wladimiroff. The other matters that we need to consider, though, are just general matters, matters which we had discussed before our recess. We want to find out where the parties are and thereafter we then will consider the application of the Prosecutor, is that correct? You do want us to consider the application this morning, if possible ---

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If possible, yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: -- in camera, and then that will not be the next witness so after that we will continue with a witness in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So we will stand in recess for 20 minutes. (11.25 a.m.) (Adjourned for a short time) (11.45a.m. (Closed session)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: (1.45 p.m.). (Luncheon Adjournment) (2.15 p.m.). (Open session)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, I thought that I might mention the fact that we have received an updated Prosecution witness list.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That, I think, might be of interest. The new list that you have given us has significantly reduced the estimated time that you will need for direct. So you now anticipate that, perhaps, the Prosecutor will complete its case in chief by when?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: About mid August, we think, yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. Thank you for giving attention to that matter. We understand that you have a heavy burden and it is not our desire to cut you off, but we want to move as expeditiously and fairly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The other matter that I need to address is that I had stated before our lunch recess that the minutes of the plenary meetings of the Judges are public and they are not public. Mr. Wladimiroff is shaking his head saying, "I know, I have probably tried to get those minutes and they said no".

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I was happily satisfied hearing you saying that because I found at an earlier stage they were not.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: No, no. We have our meetings and then sometimes we go into camera where we are totally alone, but none of those deliberations are public, and for a correct reason. There are private deliberations on Rules and a number of other matters. They state different Judges’ opinions about Rules and approaches to things that are confidential. I do not mind sharing my opinions because whatever I say in private I say in public, so I have no problem revealing my own thoughts about the Rules, but it is not appropriate to ascribe to any of the other Judges any matters that they may have said. That I did not do, but I am incorrect, they are not public. So we are now public, Mr. Niemann, would you call your next witness, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Just before I do, there is one matter I wanted to correct, if I may? I misspoke when I said earlier this morning that we had written a letter to IFOR. In fact, what had happened is that the letter was drafted but not sent because we already knew the answer. We had asked the question and had been informed it was not within their mandate. I just wanted to correct the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You do as you wish. If you keep asking, you think you will get a different answer? No, I guess not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is worth a try, your Honour. I call Sead Halvadzic. MR. SEAD HALVADZIC, called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Sir, would you stand and take the oath, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. (The witness was sworn)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You may be seated. Thank you. Examined by MR. NIEMANN

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is your name Sead Halvadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you born on 1st November 1972?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you born in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from the time when you joined the army, did you spend all of your life up until 1992 in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you attend primary school in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then when did you go into the army, into the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: March '91.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you in the army until when, what time, period of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until 15th May 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were in the JNA were you located at a town called Nis in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you trained by the army as a parachutist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In whether I was a parachutist?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Were you a parachutist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you leave the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May 15th '92.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened then, where did you go then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you go to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was orders came that all the Bosnians were to be posted back in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you returned to Banja Luka what did you do then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We stayed at the airport in Banja Luka for about one hour and a half and then the Colonel, the Commander of the airport told us that we had a week free, a week off, because there were Muslims and Croats in that unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you then return to Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you went to back to Prijedor what did you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I arrived in Prijedor I saw that Prijedor was already in Serb hands. There were Serb flags everywhere. The tanks had been painted blue and the militia APCs had been painted blue and they all had belonged to the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what did you do when you saw this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I spent at home some three days. I stayed at home and then I went to Carakovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I do not understand what the witness means by saying "they all had to belong to the JNA".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did you mean when you said that you all had to belong to the JNA in your evidence a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because the police in Prijedor, and generally the police never had any tanks or APCs or that kind of APCs never existed in the police, which means that they had been taken from the army, that the army had given them to the police and to have them painted blue as the army of -- as the police of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that after spending sometime in Prijedor you then left Prijedor. Why did you do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wanted to fight for the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you join a force of men who were doing this, who were fighting for Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were these men located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were located in a village called Carakovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far is that approximately from Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About four or five kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the name of this group of men that you joined? Did they have a particular name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the nationality or ethnic makeup of most of the members of this group of men that you joined?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were a couple of Croats and the rest were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were you armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had a couple of submachine guns, two or three snipers and a couple of bombs, a couple of grenades -- nothing else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any uniforms issued to you or did you wear any uniforms when you were with this group of men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, perhaps a couple of us had uniforms. Others wore civilian clothes or perhaps shirts that were usually worn by reserves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay with this group of men for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until the attack on Prijedor which was May 31st and then we tried to break through to Bihac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you successful when you did this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They captured me and my friend, Jasmin Adic, by a place called C'ele which is near Agic'i which is more or less midway between Prijedor and Bihac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how far is that from Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, some 20, 30 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember the date it was that you were captured?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: June 6th '92.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who captured you? Who was it that captured you on 6th June 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serbs from that locality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These were Serb soldiers, were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serb reserves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did they take you once they captured you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They took us to, what-its-name, to their Local Commune.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the name of that? You may not remember the name. Do you remember the name of the Local Commune that you were taken to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the municipality of C'ele.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From there where did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They wanted to kill us there straightaway but, fortunately, the military police and police from Bosanski Novi came and later on they transferred us to the police headquarters in Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long were you kept in Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We spent two nights there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you go from there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the second night, in the morning, they took us to the Hotel Una in Bosanski Novi, that was the military police, and at noon we were transferred to the barracks in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say the "barracks" what do you mean by that? Was that the police barracks or the military barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Military barracks in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us approximately where that is located in the city of Prijedor, the military barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At Urije.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What date was it when you arrived at Prijedor barracks? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After June 9th, it was 8th June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately what time did you arrive there? Was it in the morning or the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, between noon and afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived there what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then they took us to the first floor, left me and Burdo to stay there. Two guards were with us. One of them went to report to their Commander, to tell them that we arrived. Another one came along, saw us there and said, "What are you Ustasha doing here?" He forced us to raise three fingers and put us against the wall. Then another one said, "Tadic, do you see Ustashi?" one of them said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were facing the wall when this happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes, we were lined up against the wall with three fingers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then two men came in, one was taller, another one was shorter. They both were in camouflage uniforms with white slings, and the moment I turned somebody hit me. It was a very strong karate blow.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was it that you knew that it was a karate blow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I had also trained karate and while doing my army service I was also learning jujitso and other marshal arts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened then after you were hit with this karate blow? What happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They went on beating us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see the faces of the men that were beating you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, for a very short while.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear them speak to each other at any time during the course of this beating?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They simply struck us all the time and told us to turn to the wall with three fingers against the wall, and they hit us with their boots, with their batons and other things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any one of them use a weapon towards you at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the Commander left the building. He said, "Tadic, let those people alone", and he said, "They all have to, all their throats should be cut. That is the only way".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who said that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, but just tell us again who told them to stop the fighting.
